title: Claude Mock Exam — Set 7
description: A final mixed mock: data-level access controls, static stability and recovery automation, streaming analytics and cost governance.

responseTypes: Multiple choice: one correct response and three distractors
Multiple response: two or more correct responses out of five or more options

questions.prompt: A company is launching a new application on Amazon RDS for MySQL with gp3 storage. The database will start with about 150 GiB of data and is expected to grow unevenly to about 3 TiB over the next 3 years. The company wants to avoid paying for unused storage and wants to avoid outages caused by the database running out of space, with the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Allocate 200 GiB of storage and enable RDS storage autoscaling with a maximum storage threshold of 4 TiB.
options.B: Allocate 3 TiB of storage when the DB instance is created so that the database never needs to be resized.
options.C: Allocate 200 GiB of storage and create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on FreeStorageSpace that notifies an administrator to increase storage manually.
options.D: Allocate 200 GiB of storage and schedule an AWS Lambda function that doubles the allocated storage every 6 months.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **Grow on demand:** RDS storage autoscaling automatically increases allocated storage when free space runs low (for example, below 10% for 5 minutes), up to the maximum storage threshold that you set, with no downtime.
* **Pay for what is needed:** Starting at 200 GiB avoids paying for nearly 3 TiB of empty storage in the early years, and growth is handled automatically even if it is uneven.
* **Storage cannot shrink:** Allocated RDS storage cannot be reduced later, so over-allocating up front permanently locks in cost.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** Allocating 3 TiB on day one means paying for about 20 times more storage than needed for a long time, and RDS storage cannot be decreased later.
* **Option C is incorrect:** A manual process adds operational overhead and risks an outage if the alarm is missed or the resize is delayed.
* **Option D is incorrect:** A fixed schedule ignores actual usage: it can over-provision when growth is slow or run out of space when growth is fast, and it is custom code to maintain.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** 'Unpredictable database storage growth' + 'avoid running out of space' + 'least overhead' = RDS storage autoscaling with a maximum threshold.
2. **Right-size storage:** Determining when storage auto scaling is required is an explicit exam skill; start small when growth is uncertain.
3. **Aurora difference:** Aurora cluster storage grows (and shrinks) automatically and is billed for what is used, so no allocation is needed.

questions.prompt: A company moved all 12 of its Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL clusters to the Aurora I/O-Optimized storage configuration last year. A cost review shows that 10 of the clusters are mainly large, rarely updated reference datasets with very low read and write I/O, and their estimated I/O charges under Aurora Standard would be less than 5% of their total Aurora cost. The other 2 clusters are write-heavy OLTP databases whose I/O charges would be about 40% of their cost under Aurora Standard. Which action will reduce Aurora costs the MOST without reducing performance?

options.A: Purchase Reserved DB instances for all 12 clusters while keeping the I/O-Optimized configuration.
options.B: Switch all 12 clusters back to the Aurora Standard configuration.
options.C: Switch the 10 low-I/O clusters to the Aurora Standard configuration and keep the 2 write-heavy clusters on Aurora I/O-Optimized.
options.D: Convert all 12 clusters to Aurora Serverless v2 with the I/O-Optimized configuration.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option C is Correct

* **How the two configurations are priced:** Aurora I/O-Optimized has no per-request I/O charges but higher instance and storage prices. Aurora Standard has lower instance and storage prices plus pay-per-request I/O charges.
* **Low-I/O clusters pay a premium on I/O-Optimized:** For the 10 large, low-I/O clusters, the higher storage and instance prices of I/O-Optimized far exceed the small I/O charges they would pay under Standard, so switching them saves money with no performance change.
* **High-I/O clusters benefit from I/O-Optimized:** AWS guidance is that I/O-Optimized is cost-effective when I/O charges exceed about 25% of total Aurora spend; at about 40%, the 2 OLTP clusters should stay on I/O-Optimized.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Reserved DB instances discount instance hours but do not change the higher storage price of I/O-Optimized for the large low-I/O clusters, so the main saving is missed. Reservations can be added after choosing the right configuration.
* **Option B is incorrect:** Moving the 2 write-heavy clusters to Standard would increase their cost because their I/O charges would be about 40% of their spend.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Serverless v2 does not lower storage cost, and these are steady or storage-heavy workloads where provisioned instances are not the problem.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** 'I/O charges above about 25% of Aurora spend' = Aurora I/O-Optimized; 'large storage, low I/O' = Aurora Standard.
2. **Choose per cluster:** The storage configuration is set per cluster, so evaluate each cluster's I/O share (for example, in Cost Explorer or the CUR) instead of applying one choice to the whole fleet.
3. **Switching:** The configuration can be changed on an existing cluster; switching to I/O-Optimized is allowed once every 30 days, and switching back to Standard is allowed at any time.

questions.prompt: A payments company sends transaction events to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue. Events for the same customer account must be processed in order and exactly once, but there are millions of accounts and ordering across accounts does not matter. Peak load has grown to about 20,000 messages per second, and producers now receive throttling errors because the queue is limited to 300 API calls per second for each action. The producers already set the account ID as the message group ID. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Replace the FIFO queue with an SQS standard queue and use the account ID as a message attribute so that consumers can sort the messages by account before processing.
options.B: Create several FIFO queues and have each producer pick a queue at random for every message, with consumers reading from all of the queues.
options.C: Increase the visibility timeout and turn on long polling for the FIFO queue so that consumers make fewer API calls and free capacity for the producers.
options.D: Enable high throughput mode for the FIFO queue, which sets the deduplication scope and the FIFO throughput limit to the message group level.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option D is Correct

* **High throughput FIFO:** With high throughput mode, the deduplication scope is set to messageGroup and the FIFO throughput limit to perMessageGroupId, so throughput scales across message groups far beyond the default 300 transactions per second.
* **Ordering preserved:** Order and exactly-once processing are still guaranteed within each message group (account), which is all the requirement needs.
* **Many groups = more parallelism:** Millions of distinct account IDs spread the load across partitions, which is what lets high throughput mode scale.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** A standard queue provides at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, so consumers could not guarantee exactly-once, in-order processing per account.
* **Option B is incorrect:** Picking a queue at random would place messages for the same account in different queues and break per-account ordering.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Long polling and visibility timeouts affect consumers, not the send limit that is throttling the producers.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **FIFO throughput:** Default FIFO: 300 API calls per second per action (3,000 messages per second with batching). High throughput mode raises this substantially, scaling with the number of message groups.
2. **Design tip:** Choose a high-cardinality message group ID (such as account ID) to get both ordering and parallelism.

questions.prompt: A company runs a legacy UDP-based service on 6 Amazon EC2 instances, each with its own Elastic IP address. The client software resolves a DNS name and then connects to one of the returned IP addresses, and it already retries with another address if a server does not respond. The company does not want to add a load balancer. It wants DNS to return several IP addresses but never return addresses of servers that fail health checks. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Create Route 53 multivalue answer records, one for each instance's IP address, and associate a health check with each record.
options.B: Create a single Route 53 simple routing record that contains all 6 IP addresses, and associate a health check with the record.
options.C: Create Route 53 failover routing records with one instance as the primary and the other instances as secondary records.
options.D: Create Route 53 latency-based routing records for each instance so that clients are always sent to the fastest server.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **Multivalue answer routing:** Route 53 responds to each query with up to eight healthy records chosen at random, giving simple DNS-level distribution.
* **Health-aware:** Each record can have its own health check, and Route 53 returns only the IP addresses of healthy servers.
* **Client-side retry:** Because clients receive several addresses, they can try another one if the first fails.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** Simple routing records cannot be associated with health checks, so an unhealthy server's IP address would still be returned.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Failover routing sends all traffic to a single primary while it is healthy, so the load is not spread across the servers.
* **Option D is incorrect:** All instances are in the same Region, so latency-based routing does not help, and it returns a single answer per query.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Multivalue vs. load balancer:** Multivalue answer routing is not a replacement for ELB, but it improves availability for clients that can retry across several IP addresses.
2. **Routing policies with health checks:** Failover, weighted, latency, geolocation, and multivalue records can use health checks; simple records cannot.

questions.prompt: A company is launching a log analytics and search feature for a new product. Ingestion volume and query load are unknown and expected to spike unpredictably during incidents. Engineers want to use OpenSearch APIs and OpenSearch Dashboards, but the team does not want to choose instance types, size clusters, manage shards, or perform capacity planning. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Create an Amazon OpenSearch Service provisioned domain sized for the expected peak and enable dedicated master nodes.
options.B: Create an Amazon OpenSearch Service provisioned domain with UltraWarm nodes to handle ingestion spikes.
options.C: Create an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection of the time series type and ingest the logs into it.
options.D: Store the logs in Amazon S3 and query them with Amazon Athena.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option C is Correct

* **No cluster management:** OpenSearch Serverless removes the need to choose instance types, size clusters, or manage shards and indexes' underlying capacity.
* **Automatic scaling:** Compute capacity for indexing and search is measured in OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs) and scales automatically and independently with the workload.
* **Fits the use case:** Time series collections are optimized for log analytics, and collections support OpenSearch APIs and OpenSearch Dashboards.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** A provisioned domain requires the team to size instances and shards and plan capacity, and sizing for an unknown peak is guesswork that wastes money when idle.
* **Option B is incorrect:** UltraWarm is a lower-cost storage tier for read-only, less frequently accessed indexes; it does not absorb ingestion spikes and still requires domain sizing.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Athena runs SQL queries on S3 but does not provide OpenSearch APIs, full-text search relevance, or OpenSearch Dashboards.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** "OpenSearch without managing clusters, unpredictable load" -> OpenSearch Serverless; "keep large volumes of older logs searchable at low cost" -> UltraWarm/cold storage on a provisioned domain.
2. **Serverless pattern:** When the requirement says no capacity planning and unpredictable load, prefer the serverless version of the service.

questions.prompt: A company runs an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster. A cron job creates a manual cluster snapshot every hour, and all manual snapshots are kept for 1 year, which has made snapshot storage a major cost. The company's requirements are the ability to restore to any point in time within the last 14 days and one snapshot per month retained for 1 year. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Enable Aurora Backtrack with a 14-day backtrack window.
options.B: Set the cluster's automated backup retention period to 14 days and use point-in-time restore for recovery.
options.C: Export the hourly snapshots to Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format and delete the snapshots.
options.D: Create an AWS Backup plan that takes a monthly backup of the cluster with a 12-month retention period, and then stop the cron job and delete the hourly manual snapshots.
options.E: Increase the automated backup retention period to 365 days and delete all manual snapshots.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Options B & D are Correct

* **Option B - continuous automated backups:** Aurora automated backups are continuous and incremental and support point-in-time restore to any second within the retention period (1-35 days). A 14-day retention exactly meets the PITR requirement without storing hourly full snapshots.
* **Option D - monthly retention with AWS Backup:** An AWS Backup plan creates one snapshot per month and deletes each one automatically after 12 months, replacing about 8,760 retained hourly snapshots with 12 monthly ones.
* **Retention matched to requirements:** Snapshot frequency and retention should match the actual recovery requirements; anything beyond them is pure cost.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Backtrack supports a maximum window of 72 hours, cannot meet a 14-day requirement, and is not a backup (it rewinds the same cluster).
* **Option C is incorrect:** Snapshot exports to S3 are for analytics; an exported Parquet copy cannot be restored as an Aurora cluster, so recovery requirements would not be met.
* **Option E is incorrect:** The maximum automated backup retention period is 35 days, so 365 days is not possible.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** 'Point-in-time recovery within N days (N <= 35)' = automated backups. 'Monthly/yearly copies for long retention' = AWS Backup plan or manual snapshots with a lifecycle.
2. **Limits to remember:** Automated backup retention: 1-35 days. Aurora Backtrack: up to 72 hours, Aurora MySQL only.
3. **Snapshot exports:** Exporting snapshots to S3 (Parquet) is for querying with Athena or other analytics tools, not for restore.

questions.prompt: A logistics company exposes a shipment-tracking REST API through Amazon API Gateway. Fifty partner companies will call the API from their own backend servers, with no human users involved. Each partner must receive its own credentials that can be revoked individually, and the access tokens must be short-lived and limited to either read-only or read-write scopes. Partners do not have AWS accounts. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create an IAM user with access keys for each partner, and allow execute-api:Invoke in each user's policy.
options.B: Create an API key for each partner, and associate the keys with a usage plan for the API.
options.C: Create a Cognito identity pool that allows unauthenticated identities, and give the unauthenticated role permission to invoke the API.
options.D: Create a resource server with custom scopes in an Amazon Cognito user pool, create an app client with a client secret for each partner that uses the client credentials grant, and configure a Cognito user pool authorizer on the API that requires the scopes.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option D is Correct

* **Machine-to-machine OAuth 2.0:** The client credentials grant lets a backend system exchange its client ID and secret for a short-lived access token from the Cognito token endpoint. No user sign-in is involved.
* **Scopes and revocation:** Custom scopes on a resource server limit what each token allows. Each partner has its own app client, which can be deleted or have its secret rotated on its own.
* **Built-in validation:** The API Gateway Cognito authorizer checks the token signature, expiry, and required scopes without custom code.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** IAM users with long-term access keys for external parties go against best practices, and the keys are not short-lived.
* **Option B is incorrect:** API keys are for usage plans and throttling. AWS states that they should not be used for authentication or authorization, and they do not expire on their own.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Unauthenticated identities give anyone who uses the app the same access. They do not identify or separate partners.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Server-to-server API access, no users, OAuth scopes':** Use the Cognito user pool client credentials grant (machine-to-machine).
2. **'End users sign in to an app':** Use the authorization code grant with a Cognito user pool.
3. **API keys:** API keys meter and throttle callers. They do not secure an API.

questions.prompt: A mobile fitness app stores workout history in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table's partition key is the user's Amazon Cognito identity ID. The app uses a Cognito identity pool to obtain temporary AWS credentials and calls DynamoDB directly without a backend service. Each user must be able to read and write only the items that belong to that user. What should a solutions architect do?

options.A: Create a separate DynamoDB table for each user, and use the identity pool's role mapping to map users to tables.
options.B: Encrypt each user's items with a different AWS KMS key, and grant each user permission to use only that user's key.
options.C: Attach a policy to the identity pool's authenticated role that allows the DynamoDB item actions with a condition that dynamodb:LeadingKeys equals ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}.
options.D: Attach a resource-based policy to the DynamoDB table that allows access only from the IP address of each user's device.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option C is Correct

* **Fine-grained access control:** The dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition key limits access to items whose partition key value matches the condition.
* **Policy variable:** ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} resolves to the caller's Cognito identity ID at request time. One role and one policy therefore work for millions of users.
* **Serverless and secure:** Users receive temporary, scoped credentials from the identity pool. No backend is needed to enforce row-level isolation.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** One table per user does not scale, quickly reaches table quotas, and adds a lot of management overhead.
* **Option B is incorrect:** Encryption at rest with KMS is applied at the table level in DynamoDB. You cannot use a different KMS key for each item, and encryption does not control which items a caller can read.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Mobile device IP addresses change constantly and are often shared through carrier NAT. IP-based rules cannot reliably identify a user.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Users access only their own items in DynamoDB':** Use an IAM policy with the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition and a web identity policy variable.
2. **Column-level restriction:** Use the dynamodb:Attributes condition key to limit which attributes a caller can read.
3. **Pattern:** A Cognito identity pool plus fine-grained IAM conditions gives per-user data isolation without a backend tier.

questions.prompt: A company's public API uses Amazon API Gateway to invoke an AWS Lambda function through an alias named live. The team wants to release a new function version by sending 10% of invocations to it for an hour while monitoring errors, and to be able to return all traffic to the current version immediately if problems appear. The team does not want to deploy a second API or change the API Gateway integration during the release. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Update the $LATEST version of the function with the new code, and use reserved concurrency to limit how many invocations the new code can receive.
options.B: Create a second Lambda function for the new code, and add a second API Gateway stage that invokes it so that 10% of clients can be moved to the new stage.
options.C: Publish the new code as a new version, and give the live alias a routing configuration that sends 10% of invocations to the new version.
options.D: Publish the new code as a new version, and create Amazon Route 53 weighted records that send 10% of requests to the new version's function URL.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option C is Correct

* **Weighted aliases:** A Lambda alias can point to two versions with a routing configuration that sends a chosen percentage of invocations to the additional version.
* **No integration change:** API Gateway keeps invoking the same alias ARN, so the canary happens entirely inside Lambda.
* **Instant rollback:** Removing the additional version weight (or pointing the alias back to the old version) returns all traffic to the current version immediately.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Changing $LATEST affects every caller that uses it, gives no percentage-based split, and reserved concurrency does not route a share of traffic to new code.
* **Option B is incorrect:** A second function and stage requires clients or API configuration to change and does not give a controlled 10% split.
* **Option D is incorrect:** The API invokes the function through API Gateway, not through function URLs, so DNS weights would not affect this traffic, and DNS caching slows rollback.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Versions and aliases:** Versions are immutable snapshots; aliases are stable pointers that callers use and that can split traffic between two versions.
2. **Safe serverless releases:** Use weighted aliases for canary or linear traffic shifting with fast rollback.

questions.prompt: A penetration test showed that a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw in a web application could read IAM role credentials from the EC2 instance metadata service by using IMDSv1. A company with 40 accounts in AWS Organizations wants to make sure that all running instances use IMDSv2 only, that new instances use IMDSv2 by default even when a launch template does not specify it, and that no one can launch or reconfigure an instance to allow IMDSv1. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)

options.A: Modify the metadata options of all existing instances to set HttpTokens to required.
options.B: Turn off the instance metadata service on every instance so that no credentials can be retrieved.
options.C: Attach an SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances unless the ec2:MetadataHttpTokens condition key is required, and denies ec2:ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions requests that would allow IMDSv1.
options.D: Add an outbound security group rule on each instance that denies traffic to 169.254.169.254.
options.E: Set the account-level default for instance metadata options to require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens required) in every account and Region in use.
options.F: Replace the instance profiles with IAM user access keys stored in a configuration file on each instance.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Options A, C & E are Correct

* **Fix running instances:** Changing HttpTokens to required on existing instances (ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions) turns off IMDSv1 without a restart. IMDSv2 needs a session token from a PUT request, which typical SSRF flaws cannot obtain.
* **Secure default:** The EC2 account-level instance metadata defaults apply to new launches that do not set the metadata options themselves, so IMDSv2 becomes the default.
* **Guardrail:** An SCP that uses ec2:MetadataHttpTokens stops anyone, including account administrators, from launching or changing instances to allow IMDSv1.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** Applications and the AWS SDK on the instances need the metadata service to get the instance role's temporary credentials. Turning it off breaks them.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Security groups support only allow rules, not deny rules. Instance metadata traffic is also not controlled by security groups.
* **Option F is incorrect:** Long-term access keys on disk are less secure than temporary role credentials and can be stolen through the same flaw.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'SSRF + instance credentials':** Require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required).
2. **Enforcement layers:** Fix existing instances, set secure defaults for new ones, and add a preventive SCP guardrail. AWS Config rules can detect drift.
3. **Hop limit:** Keep the IMDSv2 response hop limit at 1 unless containers on the host need metadata access.

questions.prompt: An administrator accidentally deleted a production Amazon DynamoDB table during a cleanup task. The company now requires that production tables cannot be deleted unless that protection is explicitly turned off first, and that each table can be restored in a second AWS Region from daily backups retained for 90 days, even if the primary Region is unavailable. The company wants the MOST cost-effective solution. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Enable deletion protection on each production table.
options.B: Enable point-in-time recovery on each table with the maximum recovery period.
options.C: Convert each table to a global table with a replica in the second Region.
options.D: Create an AWS Backup plan with daily backups of the tables, 90-day retention, and a copy rule to a backup vault in the second Region.
options.E: Enable a time to live (TTL) attribute on each table so that items are retained for 90 days.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Options A & D are Correct

* **Deletion protection (A):** When enabled, DeleteTable requests fail until deletion protection is disabled, preventing accidental deletion.
* **Cross-Region backups (D):** AWS Backup (with advanced DynamoDB backup features) creates daily backups with 90-day retention and copies them to a vault in another Region, so restores do not depend on the primary Region.
* **Cost-effective:** Backup storage costs far less than running a full replica table.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** PITR keeps at most 35 days of history, and restoring relies on the source Region's backup data.
* **Option C is incorrect:** A global table replica doubles write and storage cost and replicates deletes and corruption; it is not a backup.
* **Option E is incorrect:** TTL deletes expired items; it does not retain or back up data.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Prevent accidental deletion:** DynamoDB/RDS deletion protection; S3 MFA Delete or Object Lock.
2. **Backups across Regions/accounts:** AWS Backup copy rules (cross-Region and cross-account).

questions.prompt: A retail company streams change events (inserts, updates, and deletes) for its customer and order records. The company wants the data lake in Amazon S3 to always reflect the current state of each record so that Amazon Athena queries return up-to-date results with ACID guarantees, and it must support schema evolution over time. The company wants a managed streaming delivery solution without writing custom merge jobs. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon Data Firehose to deliver the change stream to Apache Iceberg tables in Amazon S3.
options.B: Use Amazon Data Firehose to deliver the events as JSON objects to S3 and query the latest version of each record with Athena window functions.
options.C: Use Amazon Data Firehose with record format conversion to write Parquet files to S3, and run a nightly crawler.
options.D: Write the events to an Amazon SQS queue and use a Lambda function to overwrite CSV files in S3 for each changed record.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **Open table format:** Apache Iceberg tables add ACID transactions, row-level updates and deletes, and schema evolution on top of data in S3, and Athena can query Iceberg tables natively.
* **Managed delivery:** Amazon Data Firehose can deliver streams directly to Apache Iceberg tables and can apply insert, update, and delete operations, so no custom merge job is needed.
* **Current state:** Because updates and deletes are applied to the tables, queries see the current state of each record.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** Appending raw events means every query must deduplicate the full history, which gets slower and more expensive over time and does not provide ACID semantics.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Parquet files are append-only; this improves scan efficiency but does not apply updates or deletes, so data does not reflect current state.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Overwriting CSV objects per record is custom code, not transactional, and creates many small files that perform poorly in Athena.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** "Upserts/deletes/ACID/schema evolution in the data lake" -> Apache Iceberg tables (queried by Athena, EMR, Glue, Redshift); "stream to Iceberg without code" -> Amazon Data Firehose.
2. **Managed tables:** Amazon S3 Tables provide fully managed Iceberg tables with automatic maintenance such as compaction.

questions.prompt: A company runs analytics jobs on Amazon EMR in us-west-2. Every night the jobs read the same 20 TB reference dataset from an Amazon S3 bucket in eu-central-1. The dataset changes by less than 1% each day. The AWS Cost and Usage Report shows large inter-Region data transfer charges. The bucket in eu-central-1 must remain the system of record for European applications. Which solution will reduce the data transfer cost the MOST?

options.A: Configure S3 Replication from the eu-central-1 bucket to a new bucket in us-west-2 (using S3 Batch Replication for existing objects), and point the EMR jobs at the us-west-2 bucket.
options.B: Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point for the eu-central-1 bucket and have the EMR jobs read through it.
options.C: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the eu-central-1 bucket and use the accelerate endpoint from the EMR jobs.
options.D: Create a VPC peering connection between a VPC in eu-central-1 and the EMR VPC, and read the bucket through an S3 gateway endpoint in eu-central-1.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **Pay inter-Region transfer once:** Replication copies each object to us-west-2 once and then only replicates the small daily changes, instead of transferring 20 TB across Regions every night.
* **Local reads are cheap:** Reads from an S3 bucket in the same Region as the EMR cluster have no data transfer charge.
* **Source stays authoritative:** The eu-central-1 bucket remains the system of record; the us-west-2 copy is a read-only replica for analytics.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** With only one bucket behind it, a Multi-Region Access Point still serves data from eu-central-1, so the inter-Region transfer continues, plus request routing charges.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Transfer Acceleration adds a per-GB charge on top of transfer costs and does not avoid inter-Region transfer.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Gateway endpoints work only for same-Region S3 access and cannot be used across a peering connection; inter-Region peering traffic is also billed per GB.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** 'Repeatedly reading the same data across Regions' = copy/replicate it once into the consuming Region.
2. **Data transfer pricing:** Same-AZ private traffic is free; cross-AZ and inter-Region traffic are billed per GB; data transfer out to the internet costs the most.
3. **Move compute or move data:** Alternatively, run the compute in the data's Region if latency and data residency allow.

questions.prompt: A company's API uses AWS Lambda functions that connect to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. During traffic bursts, thousands of concurrent Lambda invocations each open a new database connection. The company had to scale the DB instance up to db.r6g.8xlarge only to support the number of connections, and average CPU utilization is now 8%. The company wants to reduce the database cost without changing the database engine. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Add two RDS read replicas and distribute the Lambda connections across them, then downsize the primary DB instance.
options.B: Create an Amazon RDS Proxy for the DB instance, configure the Lambda functions to connect through the proxy, and then downsize the DB instance to a size that fits the actual CPU and memory load.
options.C: Increase the max_connections parameter in a custom DB parameter group on the existing DB instance and enable Performance Insights.
options.D: Set reserved concurrency on the Lambda functions to 1 so that only one database connection is open at any time.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option B is Correct

* **Connection pooling:** RDS Proxy maintains a pool of database connections and multiplexes many client connections onto a smaller number of database connections, which absorbs bursts of Lambda connections.
* **Enables right-sizing:** Once connection count no longer dictates instance size, the DB instance can be downsized to match the real 8% CPU load, which reduces cost far more than the proxy costs.
* **Resilience bonus:** RDS Proxy also reduces failover time and can use Secrets Manager and IAM authentication.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Read replicas add instances and cost, and writes still require connections to the primary; the connection storm remains.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Raising max_connections on the oversized instance does not reduce cost, and each connection still consumes memory.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Reserved concurrency of 1 would throttle the API so severely that it could not serve traffic bursts.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** 'Lambda + RDS' + 'too many connections' = Amazon RDS Proxy.
2. **Connections drive sizing:** On RDS, max_connections scales with instance memory; pooling lets you choose instance size by real workload.
3. **Right-size after fixing the cause:** Fix the inefficiency first (pooling, caching), then downsize the instance or purchase Reserved Instances for the new size.

questions.prompt: A company's platform team lets application teams submit IAM policies as part of infrastructure-as-code pull requests. The security team must automatically block any pull request whose policy grants s3:DeleteBucket, kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion, or iam:PassRole, and must also block any change that grants more access than the currently deployed version of the same policy. The check must run in the existing pipeline before deployment. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Enable AWS Config rules that detect the listed actions after deployment, and use automatic remediation to remove the noncompliant statements.
options.B: Add IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks to the pipeline: run CheckAccessNotGranted with the listed actions and CheckNoNewAccess against the deployed policy, and fail the build if either check fails.
options.C: Apply a service control policy (SCP) that denies the listed actions to all accounts, and review all other policy changes manually.
options.D: Run IAM Access Analyzer policy validation in the pipeline, and fail the build on any security warning.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option B is Correct

* **CheckAccessNotGranted:** This custom policy check confirms that a policy does not grant any of a specified list of actions or resources. It fails if the policy grants s3:DeleteBucket, kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion, or iam:PassRole.
* **CheckNoNewAccess:** This check compares a new policy version with a reference (the deployed version) and fails if the new version grants more access.
* **Shift-left:** The checks run through the AWS CLI or API, so they fit into any CI/CD pipeline and stop bad policies before deployment.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** AWS Config evaluates resources after they are deployed. The requirement is to block the change before deployment.
* **Option C is incorrect:** An SCP blocks the actions at runtime for every principal, including legitimate administrators. It also does not detect policy changes that grant more access, so manual review would still be needed.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Policy validation checks grammar and AWS best practices. It cannot check for a company-defined list of sensitive actions or compare against a deployed version.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Block policies that grant specific actions before deploy':** Use IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks (CheckAccessNotGranted).
2. **'Policy change must not widen access':** Use CheckNoNewAccess. CheckNoPublicAccess finds resource policies that allow public access.
3. **Validation vs checks:** Policy validation finds syntax and best-practice issues. Custom policy checks use automated reasoning against your own security standards.

questions.prompt: A team in Account A built an AWS Lambda function that returns pricing data over HTTPS. A single service in Account B, which runs under one IAM role, must call the function. The team does not need request throttling, API keys, or other Amazon API Gateway features, and it wants the simplest setup. No other principal may invoke the function. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Create a Lambda function URL with the AWS_IAM auth type, add a resource-based policy statement that allows the Account B role to invoke the function through its URL, give the role matching permissions in Account B, and have the service sign requests with SigV4.
options.B: Create a Lambda function URL with the NONE auth type, and have the function check a shared secret in a custom request header.
options.C: Create a Lambda function URL with the NONE auth type, and attach a security group to the function URL that allows traffic only from Account B's NAT gateway IP address.
options.D: Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API with a Lambda proxy integration, and enable API keys with a usage plan for Account B.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **AWS_IAM auth type:** With AWS_IAM, every request to the function URL must be signed with Signature Version 4, and Lambda authorizes the caller with IAM.
* **Cross-account authorization:** For a caller in another account, both the function's resource-based policy and the caller's identity-based policy must allow the invocation. Only the named role can call the function.
* **Simplest:** A function URL is a built-in HTTPS endpoint for one function, with no API Gateway resources to deploy or manage.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** With NONE, anyone on the internet can reach the function. A shared secret is a static credential that can leak and is not tied to the IAM role.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Function URLs do not support security groups. IP-based restrictions also do not identify the IAM role.
* **Option D is incorrect:** This adds an API Gateway layer that the team does not need. API keys identify usage plans and are not meant for authorization.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Single-function HTTPS endpoint, no API Gateway features':** Use a Lambda function URL.
2. **Securing function URLs:** Use the AWS_IAM auth type with resource-based policies. Use NONE only for truly public endpoints, and add your own authentication in that case.
3. **Need throttling, usage plans, WAF, or custom authorizers?:** Use Amazon API Gateway instead.

questions.prompt: A company has 50 AWS accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations. Several business units share some of the accounts, so costs cannot be allocated by account. The company wants every business unit to see its costs in AWS Cost Explorer by using a CostCenter tag. Teams currently use inconsistent keys and values such as costcenter, Cost-Center, and cc-1234. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Activate CostCenter as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the Billing and Cost Management console of the organization's management account.
options.B: Activate CostCenter as a cost allocation tag separately in the Billing and Cost Management console of each member account.
options.C: Create a tag policy in AWS Organizations that defines the CostCenter key capitalization and allowed values, enable enforcement for the required resource types, and attach it to the organization root.
options.D: Enable the AWS-generated aws:createdBy cost allocation tag and map each IAM user to a business unit.
options.E: Create a separate AWS Budgets cost budget for each member account and share the budget reports with each business unit.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Options A & C are Correct

* **Option A - activate in the management account:** User-defined tags appear in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report only after they are activated as cost allocation tags. In an organization, activation is done in the management (payer) account and applies to the consolidated bill.
* **Option C - standardize with tag policies:** Tag policies define the allowed tag key capitalization and values, report noncompliant resources, and, when enforcement is enabled for specific resource types, prevent noncompliant tagging operations across all attached accounts.
* **Together:** Consistent tags plus activation give clean, per-business-unit cost groupings even in shared accounts.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** Member accounts in an organization cannot activate cost allocation tags for the consolidated bill; activation happens in the management account.
* **Option D is incorrect:** aws:createdBy identifies the creator of a resource, not its cost center; mapping users to business units is unreliable and does not fix the inconsistent CostCenter tags.
* **Option E is incorrect:** Per-account budgets do not split costs in shared accounts and do not create tag-based cost groupings in Cost Explorer.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** 'Allocate costs by team/project in shared accounts' = cost allocation tags activated in the management account.
2. **Governance:** Use tag policies to standardize tags, and consider SCPs with aws:RequestTag conditions to require tags at creation.
3. **Not retroactive by default:** Activated tags apply from activation onward in billing data unless you request a backfill, so activate them early.

questions.prompt: A company stores regulated documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Applications, partners, and administrators access the bucket through the S3 API from many locations. A new compliance rule says that every request to the bucket must be encrypted in transit, and any request over plain HTTP must be rejected, no matter what IAM permissions the caller has. Which solution meets this requirement?

options.A: Enable default encryption on the bucket with SSE-KMS and an AWS KMS customer managed key.
options.B: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket, and set the viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
options.C: Add a bucket policy statement that denies all S3 actions for all principals when the aws:SecureTransport condition key is false.
options.D: Turn on S3 Block Public Access for the bucket and the account.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option C is Correct

* **aws:SecureTransport:** This global condition key is false when a request is sent over HTTP instead of HTTPS (TLS).
* **Explicit deny wins:** A Deny statement in the bucket policy applies to every principal, including those whose IAM policies allow access, because an explicit deny overrides any allow.
* **Covers all access paths:** The control is enforced on the bucket itself, so it applies to every client that calls the S3 API directly.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Default encryption protects objects at rest. It does not stop requests from being sent over HTTP.
* **Option B is incorrect:** CloudFront only affects requests that go through the distribution. Clients that call the S3 API directly could still use HTTP.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Block Public Access stops public access through policies and ACLs. It does not check the transport protocol.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Enforce HTTPS/TLS for S3':** Use a bucket policy Deny with "aws:SecureTransport": "false".
2. **Minimum TLS version:** Add a deny on the s3:TlsVersion condition key to reject older TLS versions.
3. **In transit vs at rest:** SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS protect data at rest. SecureTransport and TLS protect data in transit.

questions.prompt: A company runs network appliances on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The appliance operating system does not allow extra agents, such as the SSM Agent, to be installed, but it does run an SSH server. Administrators need SSH access from their laptops. The instances must not have public IP addresses, the company does not want to run bastion hosts, and access must be controlled with IAM policies and recorded in AWS CloudTrail. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint in the VPC, allow SSH from the endpoint's security group to the instances, and grant administrators the ec2-instance-connect:OpenTunnel permission in IAM.
options.B: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with port forwarding to TCP port 22 on the instances.
options.C: Deploy a hardened bastion host in a public subnet with an Elastic IP address, and restrict SSH to the corporate IP range.
options.D: Assign an Elastic IP address to each appliance, and allow SSH only from the corporate IP range in the security groups.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **No public IPs or bastions:** An EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint provides private TCP connectivity from the internet into the VPC. The instances need no public IP address and the VPC needs no internet gateway for this access.
* **No agent needed:** The endpoint forwards the SSH connection to the instance's SSH server, so nothing extra has to be installed on the appliances.
* **IAM-controlled and audited:** Opening a tunnel requires the ec2-instance-connect:OpenTunnel permission, which can be limited with conditions on port or target, and every tunnel is logged in CloudTrail.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** Session Manager requires the SSM Agent on the instance, which cannot be installed on these appliances.
* **Option C is incorrect:** A bastion host is exactly what the company wants to avoid. It must be patched and monitored, and SSH access to it is not controlled through IAM.
* **Option D is incorrect:** This gives the appliances public IP addresses and exposes SSH to the internet, which breaks the requirements.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'SSH/RDP to private instances, no bastion, no agent':** Use EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint.
2. **'No inbound ports, agent available, session logging':** Use Systems Manager Session Manager.
3. **Security groups:** Allow port 22 on the instances only from the endpoint's security group.

questions.prompt: A company runs an Amazon MSK provisioned cluster with three brokers spread across three Availability Zones. A critical orders topic was created with a replication factor of 1. When one broker became unavailable during an Availability Zone impairment, some partitions went offline and producers lost data. The company must make the topic tolerate the loss of one broker or Availability Zone without losing acknowledged messages, while producers continue writing. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Add three more brokers to the cluster so that each Availability Zone contains two brokers, and keep the topic's replication factor of 1.
options.B: Use a replication factor of 3 for the topic, set min.insync.replicas to 2, and configure producers to use acks=all.
options.C: Enable tiered storage on the cluster so that older log segments are copied to lower-cost storage that is replicated across Availability Zones.
options.D: Use a replication factor of 2 for the topic, set min.insync.replicas to 2, and configure producers to use acks=1.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option B is Correct

* **Replicas in each AZ:** With a replication factor of 3 on a three-AZ cluster, each partition has a copy in every Availability Zone, so a broker or AZ loss leaves two in-sync replicas.
* **Durable acknowledgment:** acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 means a write is acknowledged only after at least two replicas have it, so acknowledged messages are not lost.
* **Keeps writing:** If one broker fails, two in-sync replicas remain, which still satisfies min.insync.replicas, so producers can continue.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** With a replication factor of 1, each partition still exists on only one broker, so losing that broker still makes partitions unavailable.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Tiered storage is for retention and cost; recent data written to a failed broker with a single replica is still unavailable.
* **Option D is incorrect:** With acks=1, only the partition leader confirms each write, so acknowledged messages can be lost if the leader fails before followers copy them, and min.insync.replicas is not enforced for acks=1.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **MSK best practice:** Use a replication factor of 3, min.insync.replicas = RF - 1, and acks=all for durable, highly available topics on a three-AZ cluster.
2. **Managed alternative:** MSK Serverless applies replication automatically when you do not want to manage these settings.

questions.prompt: An IoT analytics application writes small sensor files to an Amazon S3 bucket. All objects are written under a single prefix, ingest/, and at peak the application sends about 15,000 PUT requests per second. The application regularly receives HTTP 503 Slow Down responses during peaks. The objects must stay in the same bucket. Which change will MOST effectively allow the application to sustain the peak write rate?

options.A: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and change the application to send all PUT requests to the bucket's accelerate endpoint.
options.B: Distribute the objects across multiple prefixes, such as ingest/<hash>/ prefixes derived from the device ID.
options.C: Use multipart upload for every object to parallelize each write.
options.D: Enable S3 Versioning so that concurrent writes to the same key do not conflict.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option B is Correct

* **Per-prefix request rates:** Amazon S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix. A single prefix receiving about 15,000 PUTs per second exceeds that.
* **Scale out with prefixes:** There is no limit to the number of prefixes in a bucket, so spreading keys across several prefixes multiplies the request rate the bucket can sustain in parallel.
* **503 Slow Down:** 503 Slow Down is S3's signal that the request rate for a prefix is too high; the application should also retry with exponential backoff.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Transfer Acceleration improves long-distance transfer speed over the AWS edge network; it does not raise the per-prefix request rate.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Multipart upload helps large objects (AWS recommends it for objects over 100 MB). For small files it multiplies the number of requests and makes throttling worse.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Versioning keeps multiple versions of objects; it does not increase request-rate capacity and adds storage cost.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** "S3 503 Slow Down / high request rate" -> spread across more prefixes + retries with backoff; "slow long-distance uploads" -> Transfer Acceleration; "large objects" -> multipart upload / byte-range fetches.
2. **Know the numbers:** 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per prefix are frequently tested.

questions.prompt: A company loads data into a central Amazon Redshift RA3 provisioned cluster every 15 minutes. Finance, marketing, and data science teams all query this cluster, and heavy data science queries slow down finance dashboards. Each team must see the latest data without delay, and each team's compute must be isolated and sized or billed separately. The company does not want to copy or move data between warehouses. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Unload the data to Amazon S3 every 15 minutes and have each team load it into its own Redshift cluster.
options.B: Create separate workload management (WLM) queues for each team on the central cluster.
options.C: Restore a snapshot of the central cluster to a separate cluster for each team every night.
options.D: Use Redshift data sharing to a separate Redshift Serverless workgroup for each team.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option D is Correct

* **Live data without copies:** Redshift data sharing gives consumer warehouses read access to live data in the producer's managed storage, so consumers see changes as soon as they are committed and no data is copied.
* **Workload isolation:** Each team queries from its own consumer warehouse, so data science queries no longer compete with finance dashboards for the producer's compute.
* **Independent sizing and billing:** Each Redshift Serverless workgroup scales and is billed on its own. Data sharing is supported for RA3 clusters and Redshift Serverless.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Unloading and reloading copies the data, adds pipelines, and introduces delay, which the company wants to avoid.
* **Option B is incorrect:** WLM queues prioritize workloads but all teams still share the same cluster compute, so isolation and separate billing are not achieved.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Nightly snapshot restores create copies whose data is up to a day old.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** "Share live Redshift data across teams/accounts with isolated compute, no copies" -> Redshift data sharing; "query S3 data from Redshift" -> Redshift Spectrum.
2. **Hub-and-spoke:** A common pattern is one ETL producer cluster feeding multiple consumer workgroups for BI and data science.

questions.prompt: A company has 80 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations, and new accounts are created every month. Every internet-facing Application Load Balancer and Amazon CloudFront distribution must have a baseline set of AWS WAF rules, including the AWS Managed Rules core rule set. Application teams must be able to add their own rules but must not be able to remove the baseline. New accounts and new resources must be protected automatically. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use AWS CloudFormation StackSets to deploy a web ACL to every account, and ask application teams to associate it with their resources.
options.B: Create an AWS Config rule that detects resources without a web ACL, and send noncompliance notifications to the application teams by using Amazon SNS.
options.C: Create one web ACL in the management account, and associate it with the ALBs and distributions in all member accounts.
options.D: Designate an AWS Firewall Manager administrator account, and create an AWS WAF policy that contains the baseline first and last rule groups, scoped to the organization with automatic remediation.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option D is Correct

* **Central WAF enforcement:** A Firewall Manager AWS WAF policy creates and associates web ACLs with in-scope ALBs, API Gateway stages, and CloudFront distributions across accounts.
* **Baseline cannot be removed:** The administrator sets first and last rule groups. Account owners can add their own rule groups in between, but they cannot change the baseline.
* **Automatic for new accounts and resources:** With automatic remediation, Firewall Manager applies the policy to new accounts and newly created resources. Prerequisites are Organizations with all features and AWS Config enabled.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** StackSets can deploy the web ACL, but association depends on each team, and teams could change or remove the rules.
* **Option B is incorrect:** This only detects and notifies. It does not enforce protection automatically.
* **Option C is incorrect:** A web ACL can be associated only with resources in the same account, so a single central web ACL cannot protect resources in member accounts.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Centrally enforce WAF / Shield / security groups / Network Firewall / DNS Firewall across org':** Use AWS Firewall Manager.
2. **Prerequisites:** AWS Organizations with all features, a Firewall Manager administrator account, and AWS Config enabled in the accounts.
3. **Exam tip:** Firewall Manager is a management layer. It configures WAF, Shield Advanced, security group, Network Firewall, and DNS Firewall policies, but it does not inspect traffic itself.

questions.prompt: A subscription company must perform a follow-up action exactly 72 hours after each customer starts a free trial: an AWS Lambda function checks the account and sends a reminder. About 200,000 trials start each day. The company wants a serverless solution that does not require polling a database for due items and does not require custom scheduling code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: When a trial starts, create an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedule for 72 hours later that invokes the Lambda function with the customer ID.
options.B: When a trial starts, send a message to an Amazon SQS queue with a delivery delay of 72 hours, and configure the queue as an event source for the Lambda function.
options.C: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule with a rate expression of 1 minute that invokes the Lambda function, and have the function scan the database for trials that started 72 hours ago.
options.D: Store each trial start in an Amazon DynamoDB table with a TTL of 72 hours, and process the expired items from DynamoDB Streams with the Lambda function.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **Per-item scheduling:** EventBridge Scheduler supports one-time schedules (at() expressions) and scales to millions of schedules, each invoking a target with its own payload.
* **No polling:** Each schedule fires at its own time and directly invokes the Lambda function; no table scans or custom timer code are needed.
* **Self-cleaning:** The ActionAfterCompletion setting can delete each one-time schedule after it runs.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** The maximum SQS delivery delay is 15 minutes, so a 72-hour delay is not possible.
* **Option C is incorrect:** A rule that runs every minute and scans the database is the polling approach that the company wants to avoid.
* **Option D is incorrect:** DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items in the background, typically within a few days, so the action would not run at the exact time.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Delays by duration:** Up to 15 minutes = SQS delay queue or message timer; longer or exact times = EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedules (or a Step Functions Wait state).
2. **TTL caveat:** DynamoDB TTL is for cleanup, not for precise timers.

questions.prompt: A company is migrating 120 TB of engineering file shares from on-premises NetApp storage to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP. Linux and Windows clients access the same volumes over NFS and SMB. Analysis shows that only about 15% of the data is accessed in any given month, and that data must have SSD-level latency. The remaining data must stay in the same volumes and directory paths so that users can still open it without any changes. Which configuration is the MOST cost-effective?

options.A: Provision about 130 TB of SSD storage and set the tiering policy of every volume to None so that all data stays on SSD.
options.B: Provision SSD storage for the active data plus headroom (about 25 TB) and set the tiering policy of the volumes to Auto so that cold data moves to capacity pool storage.
options.C: Provision about 25 TB of SSD storage and set the tiering policy of every volume to All so that all data is stored in the capacity pool.
options.D: Migrate the active data to FSx for ONTAP, and move the inactive data to an S3 bucket that users access through the Amazon S3 console.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option B is Correct

* **Two storage tiers in one volume:** FSx for ONTAP has a primary SSD tier and a fully elastic capacity pool tier that costs a fraction of SSD per GB. Data in the capacity pool stays in the same volume and path and is read back transparently.
* **Auto tiering policy:** With the Auto policy, ONTAP moves blocks that have not been accessed for the cooling period (31 days by default) to the capacity pool and brings them back to SSD when they are read randomly, so hot data stays on SSD.
* **Right-size the SSD tier:** Provisioning SSD for the roughly 15% active data plus headroom avoids paying SSD rates for about 100 TB of cold data, while the capacity pool grows and is billed only for what it stores.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Keeping all 120 TB on SSD pays the highest per-GB rate for data that is rarely used.
* **Option C is incorrect:** The All policy places all user data in the capacity pool, so the active 15% would lose the SSD-level latency it requires.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Moving inactive data to S3 changes where users find it and how they access it, which violates the requirement to keep the same volumes and paths over NFS and SMB.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** 'FSx for ONTAP' + 'mostly cold data' + 'transparent access' = small SSD tier + Auto tiering policy to capacity pool storage.
2. **Tiering policies:** Snapshot-only (default): only snapshot data tiers; Auto: cold user data and snapshots tier; All: all data tiers (good for archives/DR copies); None: everything stays on SSD.
3. **Storage-size skill:** Determining the correct storage size for a workload often means sizing the fast tier for the working set, not for the total dataset.

questions.prompt: An ecommerce company stores its product catalog of 20 million items in Amazon DynamoDB. Customers need a search box that supports full-text search with relevance ranking, fuzzy matching for misspellings, and faceted filtering, and new or updated products must become searchable within seconds. The company does not want to write or maintain custom code to synchronize the data. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Add global secondary indexes on the product name and description attributes and use begins_with conditions in queries.
options.B: Export the table to Amazon S3 every night and query the export with Amazon Athena using LIKE expressions.
options.C: Enable DynamoDB Streams and write an AWS Lambda function that indexes each change into an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain.
options.D: Use the DynamoDB zero-ETL integration with Amazon OpenSearch Service.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option D is Correct

* **Search engine features:** Amazon OpenSearch Service provides full-text search with relevance scoring, fuzzy matching, and aggregations for faceted navigation.
* **Zero-ETL synchronization:** The DynamoDB zero-ETL integration uses an Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion pipeline to perform an initial load and then continuously apply changes from DynamoDB Streams, with no custom synchronization code.
* **Near-real-time:** Changes are replicated within seconds, so new and updated products quickly become searchable.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** DynamoDB indexes support exact-key and prefix conditions, not full-text search, relevance ranking, or fuzzy matching.
* **Option B is incorrect:** Nightly exports are not near real time, and Athena is an analytics query engine, not a low-latency search engine for a customer-facing search box.
* **Option C is incorrect:** This would provide search, but the company must write, deploy, and maintain the Lambda indexing code, handle retries and the initial backfill of 20 million items, which the company wants to avoid.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** "Full-text / fuzzy / log search and analytics" -> Amazon OpenSearch Service; "sync DynamoDB to OpenSearch without code" -> zero-ETL integration (OpenSearch Ingestion).
2. **Purpose-built databases:** Keep DynamoDB as the system of record and use OpenSearch as the search index rather than forcing search queries onto the key-value store.

questions.prompt: A startup is launching a new mobile game that stores player profiles and game state in Amazon DynamoDB. The company has no historical traffic data. Marketing campaigns could cause traffic to jump from almost nothing to tens of thousands of requests per second within minutes, and traffic could also stay very low for days between campaigns. The company wants to avoid throttling and avoid paying for unused capacity. Which DynamoDB configuration is MOST cost-effective?

options.A: Provisioned capacity mode sized for the highest expected campaign peak, with reserved capacity purchased for 1 year.
options.B: Provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling that uses a 70% target utilization and a low minimum capacity.
options.C: Provisioned capacity mode with a scheduled AWS Lambda function that raises capacity every morning and lowers it every night.
options.D: On-demand capacity mode.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option D is Correct

* **Pay per request:** On-demand mode bills per read and write request, so the table costs very little during quiet days and nothing is paid for idle capacity.
* **Handles sudden spikes:** On-demand tables instantly accommodate traffic up to double the previous peak and continue to adapt, which suits unknown and spiky workloads much better than reactive scaling.
* **No capacity planning:** With no historical data, on-demand avoids guessing capacity; the company can switch to provisioned mode later once traffic becomes predictable.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Sizing for an unknown peak and reserving it for a year pays for large unused capacity on quiet days, and the peak may still be guessed wrong.
* **Option B is incorrect:** Auto scaling reacts to CloudWatch metrics over several minutes, so a jump from almost nothing to tens of thousands of requests per second would be throttled before capacity catches up.
* **Option C is incorrect:** A time-based schedule does not match campaign-driven spikes and would still throttle or over-provision.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **Keyword mapping:** 'New table / unknown traffic' or 'spiky, unpredictable' = DynamoDB on-demand. 'Steady, predictable' = provisioned with auto scaling (plus reserved capacity).
2. **Switching modes:** You can switch a table between on-demand and provisioned modes (limited number of times per 24 hours).
3. **Warm throughput:** For a known launch event, DynamoDB warm throughput can pre-warm an on-demand table for an expected peak.

questions.prompt: A security team found that malware on some Amazon EC2 instances tries to resolve command-and-control domains and send data out by tunneling it through DNS queries. All instances use the Amazon Route 53 Resolver (the VPC +2 address) for DNS. The team wants to block DNS queries for known malicious domains in all VPCs, use threat lists maintained by AWS, and log the blocked queries. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Enable Amazon GuardDuty in all accounts, and turn on DNS log monitoring to find and stop the malicious queries.
options.B: Create Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule groups that use the AWS managed domain lists with a BLOCK action, associate the rule groups with the VPCs, and enable Resolver query logging.
options.C: Add network ACL rules that deny outbound UDP and TCP port 53 traffic from the private subnets.
options.D: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in each VPC with stateful domain list rules, and route subnet traffic through the firewall endpoints.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option B is Correct

* **DNS-layer filtering:** DNS Firewall inspects queries sent to the Route 53 Resolver and can BLOCK them (NODATA, NXDOMAIN, or override), ALERT, or ALLOW for the domains in a list.
* **AWS managed domain lists:** AWS maintains lists of domains linked to malware, botnet command and control, and other threats. You do not maintain threat intelligence yourself.
* **Visibility:** Resolver query logging records the queries and the actions taken. Firewall Manager can deploy DNS Firewall rule groups across an organization.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** GuardDuty detects and reports suspicious DNS activity, but it does not block queries.
* **Option C is incorrect:** Queries to the Route 53 Resolver at the VPC +2 address are not filtered by network ACLs. Blocking port 53 entirely would also break legitimate name resolution.
* **Option D is incorrect:** DNS queries to the VPC Resolver do not go through Network Firewall endpoints. Network Firewall domain lists filter HTTP Host headers and TLS SNI, not Resolver queries.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Block malicious domain lookups / DNS exfiltration':** Use Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall.
2. **Detect vs block:** GuardDuty detects. DNS Firewall, Network Firewall, and AWS WAF enforce.
3. **Central management:** Use AWS Firewall Manager to apply DNS Firewall rule groups to every VPC in the organization.

questions.prompt: A training company sells video courses. Each course is delivered as HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) with hundreds of small segment files stored in a private Amazon S3 bucket behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses origin access control (OAC). Only paying subscribers may access a course's files for 24 hours after they sign in, and the company does not want to change the URLs that the video player requests. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Use CloudFront signed cookies issued by the application after sign-in, with a custom policy that allows the course path for 24 hours and a trusted key group configured on the cache behavior.
options.B: Have the application generate a CloudFront signed URL for every segment file, and rewrite the HLS playlists to use the signed URLs.
options.C: Have the application generate S3 presigned URLs for each segment file that are valid for 24 hours.
options.D: Remove OAC and use an S3 bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject only when the aws:Referer header matches the company's website.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **Signed cookies for many files:** One set of signed cookies can authorize access to many objects (for example, everything under /courses/123/*) without changing the object URLs.
* **Custom policy:** A custom policy can use a wildcard resource path and an expiration time (24 hours), and can optionally restrict the viewer's IP range.
* **Trusted key groups:** CloudFront validates signatures with public keys in a trusted key group. This is the recommended method, so the root user's CloudFront key pairs are not needed. OAC keeps the bucket private.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** Signed URLs work but change every URL, so playlists must be rewritten for every viewer. That breaks the requirement not to change URLs and adds much work for hundreds of files.
* **Option C is incorrect:** S3 presigned URLs bypass CloudFront caching and OAC, and they change every URL. Also, if they are signed with temporary credentials, they may expire before 24 hours.
* **Option D is incorrect:** The Referer header is easy to forge and does not check subscriptions. Removing OAC also exposes the bucket.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Restrict many files, keep URLs unchanged':** Use CloudFront signed cookies.
2. **'Restrict a single file / client that does not support cookies':** Use CloudFront signed URLs.
3. **Origin protection:** Use OAC so that viewers cannot bypass CloudFront to reach S3 directly.

questions.prompt: A payments company processes cardholder data on Amazon EC2 instances. A new requirement says that decrypted card data must be processed in an isolated environment that operators, administrators with root access to the instance, and other processes on the instance cannot reach. Only code whose identity has been verified may be able to use the AWS KMS key that decrypts the data. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Run the processing code in an AWS Nitro Enclave, and add a condition to the KMS key policy that allows decryption only when the request comes with a valid attestation document whose measurements match the signed enclave image.
options.B: Run the processing on Dedicated Hosts with encrypted Amazon EBS volumes, and restrict SSH access to a small group of administrators.
options.C: Store the KMS key in an AWS CloudHSM custom key store, and give the instance role permission to call kms:Decrypt.
options.D: Run the processing code in a container on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, and store the decrypted data in a tmpfs volume.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option A is Correct

* **Isolated compute:** Nitro Enclaves carve CPU and memory from a parent instance into an isolated VM that has no persistent storage, no interactive access, and no external networking. Even root users on the parent instance cannot access it.
* **Cryptographic attestation:** The enclave produces a signed attestation document that contains measurements (PCRs) of the enclave image. KMS key policy conditions such as kms:RecipientAttestation:ImageSha384 or PCR values allow decryption only for the approved code.
* **Data protection:** KMS encrypts the response to the enclave's public key, so the plaintext is visible only inside the enclave.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option B is incorrect:** Dedicated Hosts give physical isolation from other customers, but administrators with root access on the instance can still read decrypted data in memory.
* **Option C is incorrect:** CloudHSM controls where the key material lives. It does not isolate the processing environment or verify the identity of the calling code, and any code using the instance role can still decrypt.
* **Option D is incorrect:** Fargate isolates tasks from one another, but it does not stop privileged operators of the workload from accessing data, and it provides no code attestation to KMS.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **'Isolate highly sensitive processing from admins / attestation':** Use AWS Nitro Enclaves with KMS attestation conditions.
2. **Shared responsibility:** The Nitro System has no operator access path for AWS personnel. Enclaves extend that isolation to the customer's own administrators.
3. **Use cases:** PII, PCI data, healthcare data, private key handling, and multi-party computation.

questions.prompt: A company is migrating an engineering application to AWS. Linux servers access shared project data over NFS, and Windows workstations in the same office access the same data over SMB. The file system must remain available with automatic failover if an Availability Zone fails, and the company wants a fully managed service. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Amazon EFS with mount targets in two Availability Zones.
options.B: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with a Multi-AZ deployment.
options.C: Amazon FSx for Lustre with a Persistent deployment and data repository association with Amazon S3.
options.D: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with a Multi-AZ deployment.

questions.explanation:
### ✅ Why Option D is Correct

* **Multiprotocol:** FSx for NetApp ONTAP serves the same data over NFS, SMB, and iSCSI.
* **Multi-AZ HA:** A Multi-AZ file system has file servers in two AZs with automatic failover and failback.
* **Fully managed:** AWS manages the ONTAP file system infrastructure.

---

### ❌ Why Other Options Are Incorrect

* **Option A is incorrect:** Amazon EFS supports only NFS, so Windows SMB clients cannot use it.
* **Option B is incorrect:** FSx for Windows File Server supports SMB but not NFS for the Linux servers.
* **Option C is incorrect:** FSx for Lustre is for Linux high-performance computing; it does not support SMB and is deployed in a single AZ.

---

### 💡 SAA-C03 Exam Concept & AWS Best Practice

1. **NFS + SMB on the same data:** FSx for NetApp ONTAP.
2. **File service selection:** EFS (Linux NFS), FSx for Windows (SMB/AD), FSx for Lustre (HPC), FSx for OpenZFS (NFS, ZFS features), FSx for ONTAP (multiprotocol).

questions.prompt: A company runs stateless microservices on Amazon EKS with self-managed EC2 worker nodes. The platform team spends significant time patching node operating systems, right-sizing instances, and scaling nodes.
